AREA FORECAST DISCUSSION
National Weather Service Wakefield VA
151 PM EDT Sun Sep 6 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
Lingering shower chances today. 

Small Craft Advisories have been issued for the southern
nearshore coastal waters Sunday night into Monday.

The rip current risk for the northern beaches has been changed 
from moderate to low.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
1) Low-end chance for isolated showers and thunderstorms today,
though no severe weather is expected. 

2) Much more seasonable temperatures to start the week, then warming 
up for mid-late week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 330 AM EDT Sunday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Low-end chance for isolated showers and 
thunderstorms today, though no severe weather is expected.

Early morning radar shows a broken band of light but persistent 
showers stretching from Brunswick County to Amherst County as a weak 
shortwave moves along the northwesterly flow aloft. The lightning 
has diminished from the showers and they are light to locally 
moderate in rainfall intensity at this hour. Some reporting sites in 
Prince Edward, Cumberland and Lunenburg Counties have recorded 0.05-
0.25" over the last few hours. Hi-res guidance keeps this off and on 
showery activity across the Piedmont throughout the day. Can't rule 
out a few rumbles of thunder, especially into the afternoon hours, 
but there is no severe weather expected today. Also of note, some 
patchy fog is developing this morning as well. High temperatures 
will be a little cooler where the showers stick around; currently 
forecasting around 80 degrees across the western Piedmont and low to 
 mid 80s to the east. Dewpoints will start to drop throughout the 
day today, making for a much nicer day than what we've been dealing 
with lately. Shower chances will diminish this evening as high 
pressure builds in from the north. Low temperatures Monday morning 
will make you want to open the windows as lower 60s are in the 
forecast. Cooler spots in the NW could even dip into the upper
50s. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Much more seasonable temperatures to start the week, 
then warming up for mid-late week. 

High pressure will continue to build down into our region on Monday 
allowing the pleasant weather to continue. Dewpoints will be in the 
low to mid 60s with partly cloudy skies. High temperatures will once 
again be in the lower 80s across the area. Expecting mostly dry 
conditions for Labor Day, however, hi-res guidance does hold onto a 
very slight chance of a shower across eastern areas throughout the 
day. Wouldn't allow that to affect any holiday plans though since 
the chance is very low. East-northeast winds may become a bit breezy 
towards the coast, especially Hampton Roads and south into the 
northern NC beaches. If you're ring in Labor Day at the beach, 
please be mindful that the rip current risk will likely be
significant as onshore winds increase and nearshore waves
build.Temperatures Monday night will drop into the upper 50s 
inland with mid 60s closer to the coast, making for a below 
normal night across the area. 

Tuesday looks very similar with dry conditions and highs in the mid 
80s persisting. Light winds will gradually become southeasterly 
through the day, helping keep skies mostly sunny. By Wednesday, our 
area of high pressure will start to slide offshore as a potent low 
pressure system crosses into eastern Canada and its associated cold 
front drops into the Mississippi River Valley . Here locally, the 
repositioning of the ridge over the southern Mid-Atlantic and 
Southeast will allow temperatures to warm up a few degrees as highs 
top out in the upper 80s to around 90 degrees. Dewpoints will start 
to creep back as well, but will remain well below the oppressive 
levels we saw at the end of last week. Dry conditions continue into 
the start of Thursday, but rain chances currently look to make their 
return late Thursday into Friday as a cold front moves through. As 
of now, southwesterly flow will result in Thursday being our hottest 
day of the week with highs reaching the low to mid 90s (warmest 
across the S/SW). Hopefully the cold front can knock highs back into 
the 80s to end the week.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z SUNDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
As of 150 PM EDT Sunday...

VFR conditions are expected to prevail through the 18z TAF
period. SCT-BKN cumulus should dissipate this evening, giving 
way to high clouds tonight/Mon AM. NE winds of 5-10 kt 
temporarily diminish tonight, then increase to ~10 kt (highest 
at ORF/ECG) on Monday. Gusts to 15 kt are possible. There is a 
low chc of patchy fog at SBY tonight, but not confident enough 
to include in the TAF.

Outlook: Mainly dry/VFR Monday through at least midweek behind the 
front. However, brief MVFR CIGs are possible near the coast with NE 
flow Mon or Tue.

&&

.MARINE...
As of 500 AM EST Sunday...

Key Messages:

- NE winds and seas will increase today into Monday. SCAs have
  been issued for the southern coastal waters.

- S to SW winds increase Wed into Thu with SCA conditions possible.

Latest surface analysis depicted a cold front south of the local 
waters with high pressure over the northern Great Lakes into Canada. 
Winds were NE 5-10 kt. The cold front will continue to push south of 
the local waters over the next couple of days while high pressure 
builds in from the north. The pressure gradient between the high to 
the north and the front to the south will not be very tight. 
However, enough of a pressure gradient exists for gradually 
increasing NE winds today into Mon, with the strongest winds 
expected on Mon across the lower Ches Bay and southern coastal 
waters. NE winds increase to 10-15 kt later today, eventually 
increasing to ~15 kt with gusts up to 20 kt across the lower Ches 
Bay and southern coastal waters Mon. While most model guidance sub-
SCA winds, the ARW and FV3 show a brief period of 15-20 kt winds 
across the middle Ches Bay and northern coastal waters this evening 
into early tonight. These same models show stronger 15-20 kt winds 
with gusts up to 25 kt across the southern coastal waters and 
Currituck Sound Mon. As such, while this is the high-end scenario, a 
few gusts up to 20 kt cannot be ruled out across all of the coastal 
waters. Additionally, cannot rule out SCA conditions across the 
Currituck Sound Mon, however, confidence is not high enough to issue 
SCAs there at this time. Given the prolonged period of gradually 
strengthening NE winds, seas are expected to gradually build from 2-
3 ft today to 3-4 ft across the northern coastal waters and 4-6 ft 
across the southern coastal waters (highest across the NC coastal 
waters) tonight into Mon. Seas subside to 2-4 ft Mon night and 2-3 
ft by Tue afternoon. Given the potential for 4-6 ft seas across the 
southern coastal waters, SCAs have been issued (4AM-7PM Mon for the 
coastal waters from Cape Charles Light to the VA/NC border and 1AM-
10PM Mon for the NC coastal waters).

Winds gradually diminish Mon night into Tue as high pressure builds 
in with a period of benign marine conditions expected to continue 
into early Wed. By Wed afternoon, S winds begin to increase in 
response to the warm sector from a ~992mb surface low moving across 
Canada north of the Great Lakes. The increase in winds will also be 
aided by the surface high sliding off the SE coast. S winds increase 
to 15-20 kt with gusts up to 25 kt by Wed evening before becoming SW 
Wed night into early Thu. Some model guidance has winds even higher 
(20-25 kt with gusts up to 30 kt). Will note that wind probs for 18 
kt sustained winds were around 100% across the Ches Bay and coastal 
waters with 50-90% probs for 25 kt gusts across the Ches Bay and 
around 100% probs across the northern coastal waters. As such, 
confidence is increasing in the potential for widespread SCA 
conditions from late Wed into early Thu across the coastal waters. 
Winds diminish Thu with only a weak CAA surge behind the front Thu 
night.

The rip current risk is low across the northern beaches today and 
moderate across the southern beaches. Given the stronger NE winds 
and higher seas on Mon, the rip current risk increases to moderate 
across the northern beaches and high across the southern beaches. By 
Tue, the rip current risk decreases to low across the northern 
beaches and moderate across the southern beaches.


Coastal Flooding....

NE winds gradually increase through Mon as high pressure builds in 
from the north. This will allow for primarily nuisance flooding 
across portions of the middle Ches Bay and along the Atlantic-facing 
beaches of the Eastern Shore with the higher high tides (late 
afternoon/evening) over the next couple of days. A few locations may 
approach minor flood stage (highest chance at Bishops Head and 
Bayford). As such, have issued Coastal Flood Statements for the 
aforementioned areas for this evening's high tide. Additional 
Coastal Flood Statements will likely be needed for Monday evening's 
high tide as well, but will hold off on issuing those at this
time.
